canonical_statement: The 2026 IDSA AMR Guidance provides treatment suggestions for infections caused by ESBL-producing Enterobacterales, AmpC beta-lactamase-producing Enterobacterales, carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales, Pseudomonas aeruginosa with difficult-to-treat resistance, carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii, and Stenotrophomonas maltophilia.
The 2026 IDSA AMR Guidance replaces earlier versions of the IDSA AMR Treatment Guidance.

A panel of six infectious diseases specialists with expertise in antimicrobial resistance convened to address treatment questions involving ESBL-E, AmpC-E, CRE, DTR P. aeruginosa, CRAB, and S. maltophilia.
Because antimicrobial-resistance epidemiology and antibiotic availability vary geographically, the guidance focuses on clinical practice in the United States.
The guidance outlines preferred and alternative treatment strategies with accompanying rationales based on pathogen identification and in vitro susceptibility data.
The guidance applies to adult and pediatric populations, but specific dosing guidance is provided only for adults.
The guidance states that it is current as of March 1, 2026 and will be updated periodically.
The guidance is informed by a comprehensive, though not necessarily systematic, review of the literature combined with clinical expertise and consensus opinion.
The guidance is intended to address important clinical questions for which high-quality evidence may be limited or emerging.
The introduction reports an estimated 4.95 million deaths worldwide in 2019 were associated with antimicrobial-resistant pathogens.
The introduction reports an estimated 1.27 million deaths worldwide in 2019 were directly attributable to resistant infections.
The introduction reports projections that antimicrobial resistance could cause up to 10 million deaths annually by 2050 without effective intervention.
The introduction reports more than 2.8 million antimicrobial-resistant infections occur each year in the United States.
The introduction reports antimicrobial-resistant infections lead to more than 35,000 deaths each year in the United States.
The introduction reports an estimated United States economic burden of approximately $20-35 billion from antimicrobial resistance.
Management suggestions are presented in a question-and-answer format for each pathogen.
Preferred and alternative antibiotic options are generally listed alphabetically in Suggested approach sections, while additional ranking nuance is provided in Rationale sections.
The guidance does not use GRADE methodology.
Treatment suggestions in the guidance are specific to the United States context.
The management suggestions assume that the causative pathogen has been identified and in vitro susceptibility to proposed agents has been confirmed.

When multiple antibiotics have comparable efficacy, the guidance advises considering safety and tolerability, cost and payer coverage, ease of administration, and institutional formulary availability in antibiotic selection.
Empiric treatment suggestions are beyond the scope of the guidance.
Initial empiric antibiotic selection should be informed by the most likely pathogens, illness severity, suspected infection source, and relevant patient-specific factors.
Prior microbiologic data, including organisms and susceptibility results from the preceding 12 months, should inform empiric therapy.
Antibiotic exposure during the preceding 3 months should inform empiric therapy.
Local epidemiology and cumulative antimicrobial susceptibility data for likely pathogens should inform empiric therapy.
Empiric regimens should be reassessed and refined after pathogen identification using susceptibility data and clinically relevant beta-lactamase information when available.
Distinguishing infection from colonization is essential because inappropriate antibiotic use promotes antimicrobial resistance and exposes patients to unnecessary harm.
Commonly selected empiric regimens often lack activity against CRAB and Stenotrophomonas maltophilia.

Decisions to include empiric agents targeting CRAB or Stenotrophomonas maltophilia should be individualized using prior culture results, host-specific risk factors, clinical presentation, and potential antibiotic toxicity.
Treatment durations for infections caused by antimicrobial-resistant pathogens generally need not differ from durations used for more susceptible pathogens.

canonical_statement: The guidance defines uncomplicated urinary tract infection as infection confined to the bladder in afebrile women or men.

source_anchor.paragraph: Duration of Therapy and Transitioning to Oral Therapy

canonical_statement: For an uncomplicated urinary tract infection that improves clinically despite empiric therapy lacking in vitro activity, the guidance generally does not recommend repeating urine cultures, modifying the regimen, or extending the planned course.

source_anchor.paragraph: Duration of Therapy and Transitioning to Oral Therapy

canonical_statement: The guidance defines complicated urinary tract infection as urinary infection extending beyond the bladder, including pyelonephritis, febrile or bacteremic UTI, catheter-associated UTI, or prostatitis.

source_anchor.paragraph: Duration of Therapy and Transitioning to Oral Therapy

canonical_statement: For complicated urinary tract infection and other infection types when susceptibility testing shows empiric therapy is inactive, the guidance suggests switching to a susceptible agent and counting treatment duration from initiation of active therapy.

source_anchor.paragraph: Duration of Therapy and Transitioning to Oral Therapy

canonical_statement: Immune status, adequacy of source control, and clinical response should be considered when determining treatment duration.

source_anchor.paragraph: Duration of Therapy and Transitioning to Oral Therapy

canonical_statement: Transition from intravenous to oral therapy should be pursued when feasible if the pathogen is susceptible to an appropriate oral agent, the patient is hemodynamically stable, the oral agent is expected to concentrate at the infection site, and gastrointestinal absorption is expected to be sufficient.

canonical_statement: The guidance cannot account for all individual patient circumstances and is intended to support, not replace, clinical decision-making.
The guidance is not continuously updated and may not incorporate evidence that emerges after development and before publication or review.
Application of the guidance should be individualized to the clinical context and patient characteristics, with clinical judgment remaining paramount.
For uncomplicated UTI, Table 1 suggests amikacin 15 mg/kg IV as a single dose.
For complicated UTI, Table 1 suggests amikacin 15 mg/kg IV once, with subsequent doses and the dosing interval based on pharmacokinetic evaluation.

Table 1 suggests a total daily sulbactam dose of 9 g using either ampicillin-sulbactam 9 g (6 g ampicillin/3 g sulbactam) IV every 8 hours infused over 4 hours or ampicillin-sulbactam 27 g (18 g ampicillin/9 g sulbactam) by continuous IV infusion over 24 hours.

Table 1 suggests aztreonam-avibactam 2.67 g (2 g aztreonam/0.67 g avibactam) IV once over 3 hours as a loading dose, followed by 2 g (1.5 g aztreonam/0.5 g avibactam) IV every 6 hours infused over 3 hours.
For uncomplicated UTI, Table 1 suggests cefepime 1 g IV every 8 hours infused over 30 minutes.
For infections other than uncomplicated UTI, Table 1 suggests cefepime 2 g IV over 30 minutes as a loading dose, followed by 2 g IV every 8 hours infused over 3 hours.
Table 1 suggests cefepime-enmetazobactam 2.5 g (2 g cefepime/0.5 g enmetazobactam) IV every 8 hours infused over 2 hours.
For creatinine clearance at least 130 mL/min, Table 1 suggests cefepime-enmetazobactam 2.5 g IV every 8 hours infused over 4 hours.
Table 1 suggests cefiderocol 2 g IV every 8 hours infused over 3 hours.
For creatinine clearance at least 120 mL/min, Table 1 suggests cefiderocol 2 g IV every 6 hours infused over 3 hours.
Table 1 suggests ceftazidime-avibactam 2.5 g (2 g ceftazidime/0.5 g avibactam) IV every 8 hours infused over 3 hours.
Table 1 suggests ceftazidime-avibactam 2.5 g IV every 8 hours infused over 3 hours plus aztreonam 2 g IV every 8 hours infused over 3 hours, administered simultaneously via Y-site.
For uncomplicated UTI, Table 1 suggests ceftolozane-tazobactam 1.5 g (1 g ceftolozane/0.5 g tazobactam) IV every 8 hours infused over 1 hour.
For infections other than uncomplicated UTI, Table 1 suggests ceftolozane-tazobactam 3 g (2 g ceftolozane/1 g tazobactam) IV every 8 hours infused over 3 hours.
For uncomplicated UTI, Table 1 suggests ciprofloxacin 400 mg IV every 12 hours or 500 mg PO every 12 hours.
For infections other than uncomplicated UTI, Table 1 suggests ciprofloxacin 400 mg IV every 8 hours or 750 mg PO every 12 hours.
For colistin dosing, Table 1 refers readers to international consensus guidelines on polymyxins.
Table 1 suggests eravacycline 1 mg/kg IV every 12 hours.
Table 1 suggests ertapenem 1 g IV every 24 hours infused over 30 minutes.
For uncomplicated UTI, Table 1 suggests fosfomycin 3 g PO as a single dose.
For complicated UTI, Table 1 suggests fosfomycin 6 g IV every 8 hours infused over 1 hour.
For uncomplicated UTI, Table 1 suggests gentamicin 5 mg/kg IV as a single dose.
For complicated UTI, Table 1 suggests gentamicin 7 mg/kg IV once, with subsequent doses and dosing interval based on pharmacokinetic evaluation.
For uncomplicated UTI, Table 1 suggests gepotidacin 1.5 g PO every 12 hours.
For uncomplicated UTI, Table 1 suggests imipenem-cilastatin dosed as imipenem 500 mg IV every 6 hours infused over 30 minutes.

For infections other than uncomplicated UTI, Table 1 suggests imipenem-cilastatin dosed as imipenem 500 mg IV every 6 hours infused over 3 hours if feasible, or imipenem 1,000 mg IV every 8 hours infused over 1 hour.
For creatinine clearance at least 90 mL/min, Table 1 suggests imipenem-cilastatin dosed as imipenem 1 g IV every 6 hours infused over 1 hour; an equivalent amount of cilastatin is present.
Table 1 suggests imipenem-cilastatin-relebactam 1.25 g (500 mg imipenem/500 mg cilastatin/250 mg relebactam) IV every 6 hours infused over 30 minutes.
Table 1 suggests levofloxacin 750 mg IV or PO every 24 hours.
For uncomplicated UTI, Table 1 suggests meropenem 1 g IV every 8 hours infused over 30 minutes.
For infections other than uncomplicated UTI, Table 1 suggests meropenem 1-2 g IV every 8 hours infused over 3 hours if feasible.
Table 1 states that meropenem 2 g is preferred for obesity, central nervous system infections, extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, or creatinine clearance at least 130 mL/min.
Table 1 suggests meropenem-vaborbactam 4 g (2 g meropenem/2 g vaborbactam) IV every 8 hours infused over 3 hours.
Table 1 suggests minocycline 200 mg IV or PO every 12 hours.
Table 1 suggests nitrofurantoin macrocrystal/monohydrate 100 mg PO every 12 hours.
Table 1 suggests nitrofurantoin oral suspension 50 mg PO every 6 hours.
For uncomplicated UTI, Table 1 suggests pivmecillinam 370 mg PO every 8 hours and states that 185 mg pivmecillinam is equivalent to 200 mg pivmecillinam hydrochloride.
For uncomplicated UTI, Table 1 suggests plazomicin 15 mg/kg IV as a single dose.
For complicated UTI, Table 1 suggests plazomicin 15 mg/kg IV once, with subsequent doses and dosing interval based on pharmacokinetic evaluation.
For polymyxin B dosing, Table 1 refers readers to international consensus guidelines on polymyxins.
Table 1 suggests sulbactam-durlobactam 2 g (1 g sulbactam/1 g durlobactam) IV every 6 hours infused over 3 hours.
For creatinine clearance at least 130 mL/min, Table 1 suggests sulbactam-durlobactam 2 g IV every 4 hours infused over 3 hours.
Table 1 suggests sulopenem etzadroxil 500 mg-probenecid 500 mg PO every 12 hours.
Table 1 suggests tigecycline 200 mg IV once as a loading dose, followed by 100 mg IV every 12 hours.
For uncomplicated UTI, Table 1 suggests tobramycin 5 mg/kg IV as a single dose.
For complicated UTI, Table 1 suggests tobramycin 7 mg/kg IV once, with subsequent doses and dosing interval based on pharmacokinetic evaluation.
For uncomplicated UTI, Table 1 suggests trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole dosed as 160 mg of the trimethoprim component IV or PO every 12 hours.
For infections other than uncomplicated UTI, Table 1 suggests trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole dosed as 8-15 mg/kg/day of the trimethoprim component IV or PO divided every 8 to 12 hours.
Table 1 dosing suggestions are limited to organisms and infectious syndromes discussed in the 2026 IDSA AMR Treatment Guidance.
Table 1 notes that suggested dosing for several agents may differ from United States Food and Drug Administration recommended dosing.
Table 1 directs readers to a separate source for suggested pediatric dosing of newer beta-lactam agents.
Table 1 directs readers to a separate source for suggested dosing of central nervous system infections.
Table 1 directs readers to international consensus guidelines for polymyxin dosing.
